West Coast and Western Interior... - Remaining breezy for much of the Coast with max gusts up to 45 mph in the Bering Strait Region, weaker to the east. Winds remain gusty this week, up to 30 mph through Wednesday before diminishing Thursday. - Light snow showers in the Bering Strait Region through Thurs totaling less than 2 inches, mainly near Shishmaref. Rain/snow showers in the Interior with little to no accumulation. Drier weather for areas south of Kotzebue Thursday onwards. - Temperatures continue to drop with highs mainly in the 30s this week, lows in the teens and 20s, coldest in the Interior. North Slope and Brooks Range... - The main storyline for the next week will be chilly, cloudy and periods of snow. - Snow accumulations will range from 1 to 3 inches for most spots through Wednesday, heavier west of Anaktuvuk Pass with up to 6 inches. 1 inch or less near Wiseman. - Snow shifts to the eastern north slope and Brooks Range by Thursday as a low moves east. - Temperatures cool into the mid/upper 20s for high in most spots on Tues. Teens and 20s in the Brooks Range with a 1F to 3F temperature drop each day through Thurs. Warmest spots will be from Kivalina to Point Hope, highs in the low/mid 30s.

Issued at 1140 PM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026 The latest information from the National Hurricane Center suggest Polo is still a hurricane as it moves across the Gulf of California, and the main remnants should be moving over the Panhandle area tonight into tomorrow morning. This will promote high moisture levels, with an extended period with near daily max PWATs (1.4" - 1.6"+) as indicated in the latest ensemble output. The increased moisture will combined with instability and lift from the upper level system to produce widespread rainfall now through tonight, before ending from southwest to northeast through tomorrow morning. Most likely rainfall (50th percentile) for the event ranges from around 0.5" in the far east to 3.0" in the west. High resolution models from both the HREF and REFS ensembles along with medium and long range ensembles suggest there will be at least one band of much heavier rainfall due to training storms (10 percent chance of exceeding 6", but ensemble max values over 10"), with the most favored position being from near Hereford to Dumas. The position could easily shift slightly southeast (more favoring Amarillo) or northwest (more favoring Dalhart). Areas that end up under the band of very heavy to torrential rain will likely see significant runoff and flash flooding, especially over urban and low lying areas. The best timing for this threat will be between about 22z and 06z this afternoon into tonight. Ward

Issued at 306 PM CDT Tue Sep 29 2026 Potentially significant hydrologic event will affect our CWA over the next several days, with flash flooding, areal flooding and river flooding possible. Shifts in locations and amounts of heaviest rainfall may significantly affect stream responses especially creeks and smaller streams. Greatest threat of heaviest rainfall is presently across the southeast two-thirds of CWA per latest meteorological model trends, however possible later wobbles to the north may bring our northwest counties into play again, thus we have continued the flood watch in those areas. Elsewhere, the river basins of most concern presently include the middle/lower Raccoon basin, Des Moines River basin below Saylorville Reservoir including tributaries like the North, Middle and South Rivers, and the South Skunk River basin especially downstream of the Ames area. Of those three, the Raccoon is of most concern due to recent moderate to heavy rain across portions of that basin, leading to increased soil moisture, which will allow more runoff to occur more quickly. Latest Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast System (HEFS) and QPF ensemble hydrographs, which include longer QPF time durations than our deterministic river forecasts, suggest the most likely scenario in many locations will significant within-bank rises to around bankfull, with some isolated minor river flooding. One outlier is the lower Raccoon basin where some moderate flooding is possible. If rainfall amounts overachieve then more widespread minor to moderate river flooding would be possible. Although unlikely, higher end rainfall amounts would lead to more widespread moderate to major river flooding. Refer to our HEFS or QPF ensemble hydrograph forecasts for more details.

Issued at 208 PM MDT Tue Sep 29 2026 Tropical moisture continues to fuel a shield of precipitation drifting north across New Mexico. While areas north of the Four Corners have seen a downward tick in shower coverage, HiRes guidance maintains isolated to scattered showers redeveloping across the Southwest San Juans this afternoon. As a result, expect periods of heavy rainfall due to additional showers with embedded thunderstorms possible. Localized heavy rainfall over already saturated soils will pose a threat to our steep and flashy terrain as well as recent burn scars. Storm activity is primarily favored across the southern tier of the forecast area. The convective potential wanes after sunset; however, as the closed low lifts towards the Four Corners tonight, another round of showers and thunderstorms redevelops. Embedded thunderstorms and additional rain expected through Wednesday evening maintain our concerns for flash flooding and rises on local rivers until precipitation finally exits the Western Slope Wednesday night. RFC guidance maintains a second peak at several sites, peaking around midnight due to Wednesday's precipitation. Fortunately, water levels are not anticipated to exceed previous high water marks. That being said, localized flooding and flash flooding continue to pose a threat to our southwestern Colorado communities until remnant moisture from Hurricane Polo and the closed low completely exit our region.
